::: {.why}
A model that predicts raw returns spends most of its capacity predicting the market, and a cross-sectionally demeaned label spends all of it on the thing you actually trade.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Show how much of a raw-return model's predictive power is the market factor, and what remains after demeaning.
- State which label you will use for the audit in week 34 and why.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Decompose it: fit the same model to raw forward returns and to cross-sectionally demeaned forward returns, and for the first one report how much of its out-of-sample R-squared disappears once you remove the common component. Most of it will.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Fix the protocol for the rest of the phase and write it down: the label, the horizon, the weighting scheme, the validation scheme and the metric. Freeze it in a configuration file and commit it, because week 34's audit is only meaningful if the protocol predates the models.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Note the exception: a time-series model on an index is legitimately predicting the market and should not be demeaned, so the protocol needs to say which problem it applies to.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
The modelling protocol is frozen in a committed configuration file before any model is fitted: label, horizon, weights, validation scheme and metric. Week 34's audit compares models under it without any of them having chosen it.
:::
